title: Pew Research Center Religion research and data landing page
answer: Pew Research Center's Religion research and data landing page collects short summaries of its religion research, including social hostilities, religious demographics, public opinion and government restrictions. The most useful point for an AI reader is a limitation: this source text never mentions artificial intelligence, technology or clergy attitudes toward AI in religious spaces. It therefore cannot substantiate the industry page's claim that Pew measures public and clergy views on AI in religious spaces. It is useful only as broad context on religion, not as evidence on AI adoption or attitudes.

sections.body: Pew Research Center publishes this page. It is the Religion research and data landing page, harvested on 26 September 2026. It gathers short summaries of Pew's religion research rather than presenting one full report. Its scope includes social hostilities involving religion, religious demographics, public opinion, government restrictions and religious diversity. The page does not state a single publication date, though some findings refer to 2023, 2020 or tracking since 2007. It is a broad index of religion research, not a dedicated study of technology or AI.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page reports that 55 countries had high or very high levels of social hostilities involving religion in 2023, up from 45 the previous year. It says members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remain highly religious and conservative, but signs point to demographic and social change. Some Americans still see Muslims through the lens of the terrorist attacks, yet Muslims are a growing, vibrant part of the country's political and religious landscape. Americans' engagement with others sorts into four distinct groups. About eight-in-ten U.S. Catholics view Pope Leo XIV favorably, though opinions on tension between Leo and President Trump split sharply along party lines. Six-in-ten U.S. adults say abortion should be legal in all or most cases. An interactive has tracked restrictions on religion in 198 countries and territories since 2007. Converts make up 8% of U.S. Catholics, while 92% were raised in the faith and still identify with it. Most U.S. adults who go to religious services say they have recently heard from clergy about at least one political or social issue. Americans largely do not distinguish between the morality of homosexuality and homosexual behavior. Across 25 countries, Americans are the most likely to see the morality and ethics of people in their country as somewhat or very bad. Singapore is the world's most religiously diverse country as of 2020, while Yemen is the least diverse.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives these figures: 55 countries had high or very high social hostilities involving religion in 2023, up from 45 the previous year. Very high scores in 2023 included Nigeria, India, Israel, Syria, Bangladesh and Pakistan. About eight-in-ten U.S. Catholics view Pope Leo XIV favorably. Six-in-ten U.S. adults say abortion should be legal in all or most cases. An interactive has tracked restrictions on religion in 198 countries and territories since 2007. Converts make up 8% of U.S. Catholics, while 92% were raised in the faith. Across 25 countries, Americans are the most likely to see the morality and ethics of people in their country as somewhat or very bad. Singapore is the most religiously diverse country as of 2020, Yemen the least, and the U.S. ranks first among nations with very large populations, followed by Nigeria and Russia. The text gives no figures on AI, technology or clergy attitudes toward AI.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in churches and faith organisations would find this source useful only as background on religious demographics and public opinion. It shows the kind of religion research Pew publishes, such as attitudes to religious groups, clergy mentions of political or social issues, and religious diversity. However, the source text contains no AI, technology or clergy attitudes toward AI in religious spaces. It therefore does not support the industry page's citation about Pew measuring public and clergy views on AI. A reader would need a different Pew page or report for that specific claim.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: This is a landing page with short summaries, not a full report. It does not state sample sizes, question wording or methodology. It does not cover AI, technology or clergy attitudes toward AI in religious spaces. Some findings are dated 2023 or 2020, and the page has no single publication date. It is partial and broad, so it cannot be used as evidence for the industry page's AI claim.
